query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles, limited atomic mobility during heating promotes localized compositional fluctuations and defect formation that lower the local melting point, thereby initiating premelting at lower temperatures and over a broader range compared to more uniform single‐metal or bimetallic nanoparticles.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid, homogeneous, single-phase Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles synthesized under rapid, non-equilibrium cooling conditions.
generation.intervention: Controlled heating across the premelting and melting temperature regimes using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and in situ high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM).
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under inert atmosphere with identical nanoparticle size distributions and thermal histories for both HEA nanoparticles and baseline (single-metal or bimetallic) nanoparticles.
generation.structural_mediator: Local compositional fluctuations and strain-induced defects formed during heating.
generation.mechanism: Despite starting as a homogeneous solid solution, the limited atomic mobility at the nanoscale during heating allows certain regions to segregate slightly. These segregated regions or defect-rich areas reduce the local energy barrier for melting, leading to an earlier and more distributed onset of premelting.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEA nanoparticles will exhibit an onset of premelting at a lower temperature and a broader melting temperature range relative to baseline particles. In situ TEM and compositional mapping should reveal local regions of segregation or defect accumulation preceding complete melting.
generation.baseline: Uniform, single-phase nanoparticles composed of a single metal or a bimetallic alloy showing a narrow, uniform melting transition.
generation.boundary: Applies to nanoparticles typically less than 10–50 nm in diameter produced under rapid cooling conditions where atomic diffusion is limited; may not hold in larger particles or systems processed under conditions allowing high atomic mobility.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature shifts and the extent of local segregation are not quantitatively predicted and will depend on specific heating rates and synthesis histories.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles: (a) Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles and (b) baseline single-metal (or bimetallic) nanoparticles with similar size and morphology. Heat both samples under controlled inert atmosphere conditions while performing DSC to record melting onset and range. Simultaneously, use in situ high-resolution TEM and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) mapping to observe local structural and compositional changes.
measurements: DSC curves showing onset temperature and melting range
High-resolution TEM images tracking defect formation
EDX compositional maps highlighting any local segregation trends during heating
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If HEA nanoparticles do not show an earlier onset or broader melting range relative to the baseline, or if no local compositional fluctuations or defect accumulations are observed during heating, then the proposed mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Through evaluation and optimization of the primary dendritic phase, a unique non-equiatomic alloy, Mn17Fe21Co24Ni24Cu14, is derived. The combination and concentration of the constituents are distinctive and result in a mixing enthalpy of 0.49 kJ/mol, which resembles a regular solution. The alloy solidifies and recrystallizes into a single-phase FCC polycrystal. This unique non-equiatomic alloy can be utilized for fundamental studies by evaluating the equiatomic counterpart and emphasizing concepts related to composition-microstructure-property relations. It has the advantage of excluding σ-phase forming constituents. Together, the results emphasize the importance of enthalpic contributions within the scope of HEAs. Firstly, they demonstrate that even at high temperatures, a large mixing entropy does not always facilitate mixing of the constituent elements. This is evidenced by the duplex structure that remains partitioned after high-temperature annealing. Furthermore, the results demonstrate how the variation in cooling rates (from the melt) may significantly change the observed microstructure and phases. cited_evidence.text: This simple model of particle formation demonstrates that adding more elements innately promotes a more random nanoparticle, regardless of element interactions. Naturally, this model offers an idealized perspective and does not reflect all experimental details. In reality, there will be distinct mixing enthalpies between the elements. This will introduce a preference for certain structures which is opposed by the limited mobility of atoms. This explains how a rather mixed particle is obtained in the synthesis for a five-element mixture, which is restricted in the binary case, but also sees signs of local segregation in the NMF analysis. The model relates well to the single-source precursor synthesis, where a solid precursor is reduced at moderate temperatures, hence limiting the free mobility. Extending this approach to other syntheses with similar solid, mixed precursors can thus provide a viable way to design new low-temperature approaches for small high entropy alloy nanoparticles. It can further be argued that starting with a high number of different elements favors the exploration of high-entropy material spaces. These methods require high reaction temperatures, and rapid cooling to maintain a high-entropy state at room temperature. As a result, the preparation of high-entropy nanoparticles with a single solid solution can be achieved in a non-equilibrium state by suppressing the formation of secondary phases. In 2018, a carbothermal shock method was reported by Yao et al. to alloy up to eight elements into HEA NPs with the designated composition and size. This method involves a 55-ms heating of mixed metal precursors on carbon supports at a peak temperature of 2000 K in argon and cooling at a cooling rate of ∼105 K/s. The high temperature ensures uniform mixtures of multiple elements by fission/fusion and catalytically driven particle dispersion mechanisms. This work has made an important step in the rapid synthesis of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles. However, this method can only be applied to conductive, surface-oxidized carbon support materials. Since then, more work has been reported on the rapid synthesis of HEA NPs within milliseconds to seconds, including fast-moving bed heating, electrical sparkling, Joule heating and microwave heating.
